title: 3D Shapes: Euler's Formula and Plans and Elevations
summary: Count faces, vertices and edges, use Euler's formula F + V − E = 2 to find missing values or spot impossible shapes, and draw plans and elevations of 3D shapes to scale.

blocks.title: In the curriculum
items: Understand and use **Euler's formula**, which connects the number of **faces (F)**, **vertices (V)** and **edges (E)** of a 3D shape: F + V − E = 2. (8Gg.05)
Draw the **front view (front elevation)**, **side view (side elevation)** and **top view (plan)** of 3D shapes **to scale**. (8Gg.07)

blocks.text: 1. Key words

items: face (F)
وجه — a flat surface of a 3D shape
edge (E)
حرف — a line where two faces meet
vertex, vertices (V)
رأس، رؤوس — a corner where edges meet
polyhedron (plural: polyhedra)
متعدد السطوح — a 3D shape whose faces are all flat polygons
prism
منشور — the same cross-section all the way through; two identical ends joined by rectangles
pyramid
هرم — a polygon base with triangles meeting at one point (the apex)
plan (top view)
المسقط الأفقي — what you see looking straight down from above
front elevation
المسقط الرأسي الأمامي — what you see looking straight at the front
side elevation
المسقط الجانبي — what you see looking straight at the side
to scale
بمقياس رسم — every length is multiplied or divided by the same number
isometric drawing
رسم أيزومتري — a 3D drawing on triangle-dot paper

blocks.text: Count carefully and in an organised way: **faces** — count the front and back, then the faces around the sides; **vertices** — count the corners on the top layer, then the bottom layer (or the base, then the apex); **edges** — count the edges round each end, then the edges joining the ends.
3. Euler's formula
Look at the last column of the table: it is **always 2**. This pattern was discovered by the mathematician Leonhard Euler and is called **Euler's formula**.

blocks.title: Euler's formula
blocks.text: **F + V − E = 2**   (faces + vertices − edges = 2). It can also be written **F + V = E + 2**. It works for polyhedra: shapes with flat faces, straight edges and no holes through them.
**Rearranging the formula** lets you find a missing number:
**Prisms and pyramids in general (generalising).** If the end of a prism (or the base of a pyramid) has **n** sides:
**Curved shapes do not follow the formula.** A cylinder has 3 faces (2 flat, 1 curved), 2 curved edges and 0 vertices: 3 + 0 − 2 = 1, not 2. So use Euler's formula only for shapes with flat faces.

**Compound shapes** also follow the formula, if they have flat faces and no holes. The tower below is a cube with a square-based pyramid on top. The square where they join is inside, so it is not a face.

blocks.title: قانون أويلر بالعربي
blocks.text: عدد الأوجه + عدد الرؤوس − عدد الأحرف = 2 دايمًا (F + V − E = 2) لأي مجسم أوجهه كلها مستوية ومفيهوش خرم. لو ناقصك رقم، عوّض في القانون وهات المجهول: مثلاً الأحرف E = F + V − 2. والقانون ده مش بيشتغل مع الأسطوانة أو المخروط لأن فيهم أسطح منحنية. ولو حد قالك مجسم مجموعه مش بيدي 2، يبقى المجسم ده مستحيل.
4. Plans and elevations
A 3D shape can be shown by three flat (2D) drawings, each looking **straight at** one side:

items: **Plan** (top view): looking straight down from above.
**Front elevation** (front view): looking straight at the front, from the direction marked F.
**Side elevation** (side view): looking straight at the side, from the direction marked S.

blocks.text: In each view you see only the **outline and the edges facing you**, with no depth. You draw a line wherever there is an **edge**: where the height or the depth of the shape changes. A flat surface made of several cubes is drawn as **one** region, with no lines across it.

items: **Find the width, height and depth** of the shape (count the cubes, or read the measurements).
**Front elevation:** stand at F. For each column across, how high is it? Draw that outline. Add a line wherever a nearer part stops and a part further back continues.
**Side elevation:** stand at S. Your left and right are now different! Check which end is on your left.
**Plan:** look from above with the front at the bottom of your drawing. Draw the outline of the whole 'footprint', then lines where the height changes.
**To scale:** multiply or divide every real length by the scale (for example 1 cm represents 2 m means divide metres by 2). Use a ruler and a sharp pencil; label each view.

blocks.title: المساقط بالعربي
items: Plan = المسقط من فوق (كأنك طاير فوق المجسم). Front elevation = من قدام. Side elevation = من الجنب.
ارسم خط بس في الأماكن اللي فيها حرف — يعني الارتفاع أو العمق بيتغير. السطح المستوي ماترسمش جواه خطوط.
بمقياس رسم: كل الأطوال بتتقسم على نفس الرقم. مثلاً 1 cm بيمثل 2 m ← اقسم كل الأمتار على 2.

blocks.text: 5. Worked examples

**Worked example 1** [1 mark]
A polyhedron has 8 faces and 12 vertices. Use Euler's formula to find the number of edges.
E = F + V − 2 = 8 + 12 − 2 = **18 edges**. (This is a hexagonal prism: 3 × 6 = 18 ✓.)

**Worked example 2** [2 marks]
A polyhedron has 10 vertices and 15 edges. How many faces does it have? Which prism could it be?

items: A prism with an n-sided end has 2n vertices: 2n = 10, so n = 5. It could be a **pentagonal prism** (7 faces, 10 vertices, 15 edges ✓).

blocks.text:
**Worked example 3** [2 marks]
Samira says: 'I have made a polyhedron with 6 faces, 6 vertices and 11 edges.' Explain why she must have counted wrongly.
F + V − E = 6 + 6 − 11 = 1. For every polyhedron F + V − E = 2, and **1 ≠ 2**, so these numbers are impossible. (1 mark for the calculation, 1 mark for comparing with 2.)

**Worked example 4** [2 marks]
A pyramid has 20 edges. How many faces and vertices does it have?

items: A pyramid with an n-sided base has 2n edges: 2n = 20, so n = 10 (a decagonal pyramid).
Faces = n + 1 = 11; vertices = n + 1 = 11.
Check with Euler: 11 + 11 − 20 = 2 ✓

blocks.text:
**Worked example 5** [3 marks]
A tent is a triangular prism. The front is an isosceles triangle 3 m wide and 2 m high. The tent is 4 m long. Draw the front elevation, side elevation and plan to a scale of 1 cm to 1 m.

items: **Front elevation:** a triangle with base 3 cm and height 2 cm (the top is above the middle of the base, 1.5 cm from each end).
**Side elevation:** a rectangle 4 cm long and 2 cm high (you see the sloping roof side-on).
**Plan:** a rectangle 3 cm by 4 cm with a line down the middle: the ridge (top edge) of the tent.
**Common mistake:** forgetting the ridge line in the plan, or drawing the side elevation with the sloping length instead of the height.

blocks.text:
**Worked example 6** [1 mark]
The front elevation of a building is drawn to a scale of 1 cm to 5 m. On the drawing, the building is 7.2 cm wide. How wide is the real building?
7.2 × 5 = **36 m**.

blocks.title: Common mistakes
items: Forgetting the hidden edges, faces and vertices at the back when counting.
Using Euler's formula for a cylinder, cone or sphere (curved surfaces).
Rearranging wrongly: E = F + V − 2, not F + V + 2.
Drawing a 3D (sloping) picture instead of a flat view. Each view is 2D.
Mixing up the side elevation and the front elevation, or swapping left and right in the side view.
Drawing lines across a flat surface in a plan or elevation, or missing the line where the height changes.
Not using the scale for every length (for example scaling the width but not the height).

blocks.title: How Checkpoint asks this
items: "Complete the table" of faces, vertices and edges, then "Show that Euler's formula works for this shape."
"A shape has 9 faces and 14 vertices. Work out the number of edges." Write the formula, substitute, answer.
"Explain why a polyhedron cannot have…" Show F + V − E and say it is not 2.
Isometric drawings of shapes made of cubes: "On the grid, draw the plan / front elevation / side elevation." Arrows on the drawing show the directions.
"Draw a ring around the plan of this shape" from several options.
Scale drawings: "Draw the front elevation to a scale of 1 cm to 2 m" or "How tall is the real object?" Use a ruler and label lengths.

blocks.text: Practice

blocks.title: Euler's formula, plans and elevations — practice
blocks.intro: 14 questions, from easy to Checkpoint-hard. No calculator needed. Have squared paper ready for the drawing question.

questions.q: Which is Euler's formula for a polyhedron with F faces, V vertices and E edges?
questions.e: Faces + vertices − edges = 2. Check with a cube: 6 + 8 − 12 = 2.

questions.q: A polyhedron has 7 faces and 10 vertices. How many edges does it have?
A polyhedron has 12 edges and 6 vertices. How many faces does it have?
questions.e: F = E + 2 − V = 12 + 2 − 6 = 8. (This is an octahedron.)

questions.q: How many edges does a pentagonal pyramid have?
questions.e: 5 edges round the pentagon base + 5 edges up to the apex = 10 (2n with n = 5).

questions.q: How many vertices does an octagonal prism have?
questions.e: Two octagonal ends with 8 vertices each: 2 × 8 = 16.

questions.q: Show that Euler's formula works for a hexagonal pyramid.
questions.ms: 1 mark: F = 7, V = 7 and E = 12 all correct. 1 mark: 7 + 7 − 12 = 2 shown (accept F + V = 14 = E + 2).
questions.e: Faces: 1 hexagon + 6 triangles = 7. Vertices: 6 round the base + 1 apex = 7. Edges: 6 round the base + 6 to the apex = 12. F + V − E = 7 + 7 − 12 = 2 ✓, so the formula works.

questions.q: Which set of numbers is **impossible** for a polyhedron?
questions.e: Work out F + V − E for each: A 6 + 8 − 12 = 2; B 5 + 6 − 9 = 2; C 7 + 7 − 13 = 1; D 8 + 6 − 12 = 2. Only C does not give 2, so it is impossible.

questions.q: How many edges does the tower have?
questions.e: Cube: 12 edges. The pyramid adds the 4 sloping edges up to the apex (its base edges are the cube's top edges, already counted). 12 + 4 = 16. Check: F = 5 + 4 = 9, V = 8 + 1 = 9, and 9 + 9 − 16 = 2 ✓.

questions.q: A cylinder stands on its circular base. Which view of it is a circle: the plan, the front elevation or the side elevation?
questions.e: Looking down from above you see the circular top, so the plan is a circle. The front and side elevations are rectangles.

questions.q: A solid has a triangle as its front elevation, a triangle as its side elevation, and a square with both diagonals drawn as its plan. What is the solid?
questions.e: Square base seen from above, with the 4 sloping edges meeting at the apex (the diagonals in the plan); from the front and side it looks like a triangle. It is a square-based pyramid. (A cone's plan is a circle; a triangular prism's side view is a rectangle.)

questions.p: The solid is made from 6 cubes. F shows the front, S shows the side. Four drawings, A, B, C and D, are shown under it.

questions.q: Which drawing is the **plan** of the solid?
questions.e: From above (front at the bottom): the back row has 3 cubes across; in front of it there is 1 cube at the left end. So the plan is a row of 3 squares with 1 square below the left one: B. There are lines where the height changes (the two towers are 2 cubes high). A is the mirror image, C is the front elevation, D is upside down.

questions.q: A building is 24 m long. Its front elevation is drawn to a scale of 1 cm to 4 m. How long is the building on the drawing?
The front elevation of a tent is drawn to a scale of 1 cm to 50 cm. On the drawing, the base of the tent is 6 cm. How wide is the real tent, in metres?
questions.e: Real width = 6 × 50 = 300 cm. 300 cm = 3 m (divide by 100).

questions.q: On squared paper, draw the **plan** of the solid. Use one square for each cube edge.
questions.ms: 1 mark: correct outline: 3 rows (front at the bottom) — back row 2 squares, middle row 2 squares, front row 1 square on the left (a 2-by-2 square with one extra square below the left side). 1 mark: correct lines inside: a line separating the whole back row from the middle row, and a line between the two squares of the back row (heights 3 and 2); no other inside lines. Accept the whole drawing rotated 180° only if the front is clearly labelled.
questions.e: Look down from above with the front at the bottom. The footprint: back row 2 cubes (x = 0 and 1), middle row 2 cubes, front row 1 cube on the left. Heights: back-left 3 cubes, back-right 2 cubes, the other three are 1 cube high. So draw the outline of a 2 × 2 square with one more square below the left side. Draw lines where the height changes: between the back row and the middle row, and between the two back squares. The middle row and the front square are all 1 cube high, so there are no lines between them.

blocks.title: Remember
items: Euler's formula: F + V − E = 2 for any polyhedron (flat faces, no holes). Rearrange it to find a missing value: E = F + V − 2.
Prism with an n-sided end: F = n + 2, V = 2n, E = 3n. Pyramid with an n-sided base: F = V = n + 1, E = 2n.
If F + V − E is not 2, the shape is impossible (or counted wrongly).
Plan = from above; front elevation = from the front; side elevation = from the side. Each is a flat 2D drawing.
Draw lines only where there is an edge (height or depth changes), and use the same scale for every length.
